intro: Lazur is a voice AI assistant for urban planners who work on a Mac. Hold a key, ask a question, and it answers out loud while it sees your screen. It explains terms, points at controls, guides you through steps, drafts text for staff reports and public notices, and dictates at the cursor. It does not run your GIS analysis or edit your files.

blocks.text: Where an urban planner's day actually goes

No survey we could find measures how much time urban planners spend on email, admin work or typing. So the figures in this section come from broader office studies. Read them as a rough guide to the pressure on your week, not as a timesheet for planners.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics describes the work in plain terms. Planners assess whether a developer's site plan is feasible and recommend approval or denial. They meet with officials, developers and the public. They prepare research reports and presentations, and they often use GIS software to bring data together. Each of those tasks ends in a document, a slide or a meeting.

The Microsoft figures show the message load. Its June 2025 study covered 31,000 knowledge workers in 31 markets. The average worker received 117 emails and 153 Teams messages a day. The same workers were interrupted 275 times a day by meetings, email or chat. Those numbers describe office workers in general, not planners. A planning department still runs on the same kind of inbox.

Microsoft's 2023 Work Trend Index adds a second view. It found the average employee spends 57% of their time communicating in meetings, email and chat. That figure comes from 2023 Microsoft 365 usage data, so read it as a trend, not a fixed number.
Planning tasks that fill the calendar
The BLS duty list maps well onto a planner's week. These are the tasks that turn into documents and meetings:

items: Reviewing developer site plans and writing a recommendation on feasibility.
Drafting staff reports, findings and research summaries.
Preparing presentations for hearings, boards and council briefings.
Answering questions from residents, officials and developers by email.
Building GIS maps and combining datasets from several sources.
Writing public notices and plain-language summaries of decisions.

blocks.text: Each item is a chance to save time, but not every item suits an AI assistant. A map analysis needs your GIS software and your judgment. A notice or a summary can often start as a draft from a voice prompt.
What the research says about planners and software

A 2024 JAPA study compared planners in the US, Canada, the UK, Australia and New Zealand. It found little evidence of increased or transformational use of specialist planning software. Day-to-day work looked similar across those countries.

The same study asked planners to rank technology priorities. Office efficiency and automation of bureaucratic work came first. Data technologies came second. Community engagement technology came third. The APA blog post does not state the sample size, so treat the ranking as directional.
Put simply, the stated priority is the paperwork. That is the part of the week a voice assistant can touch most directly.
Why ArcGIS Pro makes the Mac harder

If your GIS work runs in ArcGIS Pro, the Mac is the awkward part. Esri's documentation says ArcGIS Pro has no native macOS version. On a Mac you run it through Boot Camp or a virtual machine. Boot Camp works only on Intel Macs, and you cannot run macOS and Windows at the same time in that setup.
On Apple silicon, the virtual machine is the only option. Esri names Parallels 18 or later with Windows 11 ARM. The table below lists the limits Esri documents for that setup.

blocks.title: Intel support is ending
blocks.text: Esri says macOS Tahoe (version 26) will be the last macOS version to support Intel processors. Esri also troubleshoots defects only on certified Windows x64 systems. If you buy a new Mac for GIS, plan around that.
ArcGIS Pro 3.7 added layer visibility overrides per map frame and offline help through the ArcGIS Documentation Center. Ask Lazur to explain a new option before you change a map other people use.

Here is where Lazur fits. The Parallels window is part of your screen, so Lazur can see it and point inside it. Ask where the layer visibility control lives and Lazur circles it. It does not run the analysis, and it does not click through ArcGIS Pro for you.
What an AI assistant for urban planners does on a Mac
Lazur sees whatever app is in front of you, so the same help works in Word, PowerPoint, Mail and Chrome. These seven kinds of help cover most of the planning day:

items: Explain: ask what a term means, such as floor area ratio, or what an error in a report says.
Point: ask where a setting lives. Lazur circles it on screen and labels it.
Guide: ask for steps. Lazur walks you through them one click at a time and waits for each click.
Dictate: hold fn and talk. Clean, formatted text lands at the cursor in any app.
Draft: ask for a first pass of a summary, a notice or a hearing handout. You check it before it goes out.
Research: send a question to run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs. It comes back with a summary and a report.
Everyday: set timers, add Apple Reminders and Calendar events, and open apps or links by voice.

blocks.text: The list is not a feature tour. Each item removes a specific kind of interruption. Explain saves a trip to a manual. Point saves a hunt through a ribbon. Draft saves a blank page.
Dictating a staff report without typing every line
Long summaries take time to type. Hold fn, speak in full sentences, and the text lands at the cursor. Then ask Lazur to tighten each paragraph.

Two settings help with planning vocabulary. The personal dictionary holds words dictation gets wrong, such as project names, street names and council member names. Snippets hold text you reuse, such as the closing line of a standard notice. Set both up once, then reuse them each cycle.

blocks.title: Check names before they leave
blocks.text: Dictation gets proper nouns wrong. Read every project name, parcel reference and resident name before the text leaves your Mac. A wrong street name in a public notice is hard to walk back.
A worked example: prepping a public hearing

Say a public hearing is next week, and the staff report is still a draft. This sequence uses Lazur for the parts it suits. It assumes you already know your jurisdiction's notice rules. Lazur explains terms. It does not decide what your code requires.

items: Dictate the project summary into Word, then ask Lazur to shorten each paragraph to plain language.
Ask Lazur to explain any zoning term in the staff report before you write the recommendation.
Ask Lazur to draft a one-page summary for residents. Compare it with the staff report and fix any wording that changed.
Build the slide deck. Ask Lazur where the slide size setting lives, then add slide numbers so residents can follow along.
Add the hearing to Calendar and set an Apple Reminders alert for the packet deadline.

blocks.text: The slides need the same care as the report. Speaker notes keep the presenter on the facts, and slide numbers help the room find a map. Follow [how to add speaker notes in PowerPoint](/how-to/add-speaker-notes-in-powerpoint) and [how to add slide numbers in PowerPoint](/how-to/add-slide-numbers-in-powerpoint) on Mac.
Privacy, employer rules and applicant data

Planning files can hold personal data. Applicant addresses, household details and resident complaints are common examples. Your agency decides what can go into an AI tool. Ask your records office or IT team before you paste, type or dictate applicant files. Follow their answer, even where this page says something different.

Here is how Lazur handles what it sees. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Read the privacy details before you use Lazur on agency files.
This page does not make compliance claims for your agency. Your records rules, retention schedule and public records duties still apply to anything you write with help.
What to do when an AI answer is wrong

Any AI tool can misread a planning term. A word can mean one thing in your code and another in a textbook. Floor area ratio is a good example. Some codes count parking, some count mechanical space, and some exclude basements. Ask Lazur what the term means in general. Then find the definition in your own code and use that one.

Lazur answers out loud, so you may miss an exact phrase. When the wording matters, ask Lazur to draft the answer into your document, then read it against the source. The same rule applies to numbers. A figure given from memory needs a check against the document it came from. Use ⌘ F in the source to find the term, then read the section around it. If the code and the explanation disagree, the code wins. Write the question down for your senior planner or counsel.
Common mistakes when you use AI at work

items: Pasting an applicant file into a tool before you check your employer's data rules.
Trusting a figure without opening its source. Check the number in the report, not in the chat.
Asking for a legal conclusion. Lazur can explain a term. It cannot tell you what your code allows.
Expecting Lazur to run ArcGIS Pro. It points and explains. You still click and run the analysis.
Sending a draft public notice straight out. Read it aloud once, then have a second person check it.
Skipping the Mac setup. ArcGIS Pro needs Parallels or Boot Camp, so plan that before a project deadline.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes come from treating a fast draft as a finished one. The assistant speeds up the first pass. The checking is still your job.
Using research for comparisons across cities

The research capability suits questions with many sources. Ask how other cities word hearing notices for a rezoning, or how a comparable bike lane policy is written. Lazur runs the search in its own Chrome tabs and returns a summary and a report. Check each source before you cite it, and keep your own notes on which page said what.
Research is not a replacement for your agency's own code or past decisions. Use it to find candidates, then read the original document.
Setting up Lazur for planning work

Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available. Download the app from the [download page](/download), then open it once so the free trial starts. The trial needs no credit card. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) for current plans and action limits.

Learn two shortcuts first. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Hold fn to dictate. Try both on a document you already know, such as last month's staff report, before you rely on them in a meeting.
What to do next with planning documents

If your next task is a staff report, start with [Word for urban planners](/for/urban-planners/word). Revised drafts are common, so [compare two documents in Word](/how-to/compare-two-documents-in-word) to see what changed on Mac. For the hearing deck, see [PowerPoint for urban planners](/for/urban-planners/powerpoint).
Start small. Ask one explain question and one point question on a real file today. If the answers hold up, add dictation to your next draft. That order keeps the checking manageable.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with ArcGIS Pro on a Mac?
faq.answer: Lazur sees your screen, so it can see ArcGIS Pro running in Parallels. It can point at a control and explain what it does. It does not run the analysis. ArcGIS Pro itself still needs Parallels or Boot Camp on your Mac, and Esri lists limits for Apple silicon.

faq.question: Can an AI assistant write a staff report for me?
faq.answer: It can draft a first pass from your notes and tighten wording. You still own the facts, the findings and the recommendation. Check every number against its source before the report leaves your desk.

faq.question: Is it safe to use with applicant files?
faq.answer: Follow your agency's rules on applicant and personal data. Ask your records or IT office before you use any AI tool with those files. This page does not make compliance claims for your agency.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is for macOS on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. If your GIS runs on Windows, Lazur can still help with writing and dictation on your Mac.

faq.question: How does Lazur handle the screen and audio?
faq.answer: It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: How is it different from a chatbot in a browser?
faq.answer: A browser chatbot waits for you to paste text into it. Lazur sees the app you are in and points at controls in that app. You can hold a key and ask while you work in Word or PowerPoint.

faq.question: What should I try first?
faq.answer: Try the explain and point capabilities on a document you know well. Ask what a term means, then ask where a setting lives. Move to dictation once you trust the output on a few drafts.
